claims.text: Under demanding engineering service conditions, the initially single-phase high-entropy alloy loses toughness and undergoes brittle fracture.
Minor elements segregate to grain boundaries during mechanical loading.
Grain-boundary segregation of minor elements reduces interfacial cohesion.
The initial alloy is a single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial alloy displays ductile behavior under standard loading conditions.
High-strain-rate and/or subambient-temperature mechanical tests simulate demanding service conditions.
High strain rate and low temperature accelerate stress-induced diffusion and segregation.
A controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation from contributing extrinsic effects.
Segregation produces localized grain-boundary regions of reduced cohesion.
Severe mechanical loading promotes diffusion or stress-assisted migration of minor alloying elements toward grain boundaries.
Accumulation of minor elements at grain boundaries reduces the cohesive energy between adjacent grains.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion changes the fracture response from ductile to brittle.
Samples with significant grain-boundary segregation will exhibit lower fracture toughness than the untreated baseline.
Samples with significant grain-boundary segregation will transition from ductile to brittle fracture behavior relative to the untreated baseline.
The proposed behavior applies above a threshold combination of strain rate and temperature.
Rapid quenching and homogenization treatments can inhibit grain-boundary segregation.
